articles.body: HELP! I’VE FALLEN AND I CAN GET UP: A report from the New York City Department of Investigation confirmed today what many political watchers have long suspected — that the city’s police pension system is ripe for abuse. The Police Pension Fund doles out retirement payments to all NYPD officers and, in fiscal year 2025, paid $935 million to officers who qualified for accident disability retirement — meaning they were injured on the job and unable to perform their duties. While DOI Commissioner Nadia Shihata said injured officers should be fairly compensated, her office found the pension system assigns this distinction — which boosts pension payments by 50% and allows officers to receive 75% of their average pay — without considering an officer’s specific job duties. “No New Yorker wants to stand in the way of NYPD officers rightfully receiving accident benefits when they suffer injuries on the job and are unable to work,” Shihata said in a statement. “But the [Police Pension Fund’s] current administration of these benefits is vulnerable to misuse and does not employ standards consistent with those used in similar law enforcement retirement systems, such as the system for state police.” Instead, the board has a single standard: whether an applicant can perform the general duties of a police officer, like subduing a suspect or operating a firearm — a threshold that makes less sense for officers with desk or administrative jobs. The report specifically cited the case of former Chief of Department John Chell, who was awarded a $295,919 annual pension while serving as the NYPD’s highest-ranking uniformed officer under former Mayor Eric Adams. The huge sum came, in part, because of an ankle injury sustained in 2024. Chell was among several top Adams-era police officials who received lucrative payouts using this criteria, which the DOI report argued contributed to mistrust in the system and the belief that higher-ranking officers had an easier time securing disability pay . (The report did not make any assumptions about whether Chell would have been granted his pension under stricter criteria.) DOI contends this standard incentivizes more people to claim a disability, citing a 2015 report that found 21% of NYPD employees retire on accident disability compared to 6% within the state system for police and firefighters, which has a more narrow criteria for awarding disability pay. Shihata even suggested that the pension board’s broad standard might not be legal, since courts have found, in the case of the state police pension rules, that job duty means what an officer actually does in practice. Despite that, the board rejected a DOI recommendation to change the standard. Notably, DOI pointed out in its report that two of the people on the medical board making the determinations are appointed by city agencies controlled by the mayor — which means Mayor Zohran Mamdani could push to overrule the board’s leadership. City Hall did not respond to a question about whether he would do so. The NYPD declined to comment, while the pension board did not respond. Chell could not be reached. The pension system does include a safeguard to maximize city resources. The board is authorized to re-examine officers receiving disability pensions who aren’t yet of retirement age to see if their condition would allow them to work a different city job, even if it’s not in the NYPD. If they’re deemed able, then they’re primarily compensated with their pension money until they reach retirement age. So is the pension system using this provision to examine the $100 million worth of annual pension payments doled out to NYPD officers who are under the retirement age, which the board is required by law to do? In short, no. Since 2019, the board has only reevaluated one pensioner, per the DOI report. And that person was found unable to do any other city work. The report found examples indicating the board could be doing a more thorough job. DOI provided findings that suggest four officers under the retirement age are receiving disability pensions while engaging in activities like lifting weights, performing home renovations, playing competitive sports, doing pushups, instructing workout classes and, in one case, performing “complicated dance routines exhibiting a full range of arm motion.” DOI recommended the board require officers receiving disability payments who are not yet of retirement age to periodically certify they still have a disability. The board rejected this recommendation, but agreed to create an online portal to gain input from the public on pensioners who may be healthy enough to work. It also agreed to reevaluate the four retirees flagged by DOI. — Joe Anuta From the Capitol META’S DAY IN COURT: New York’s top court opened its fall session this afternoon with a case that could have massive implications for the legal liability of social media companies and AI users. Website owners are typically immune from liability for content created by third parties. But the families of the 2022 mass shooting in Buffalo are arguing that social media companies shouldn’t dodge responsibility for radicalizing Payton Gendron, the 18-year-old who drove across the state with the goal of killing Black people. The state Court of Appeals is now deciding whether these families can proceed with a lawsuit against companies such as Meta, Google, Discord, Reddit, Amazon and 4Chan. Gendron’s diaries and confessions show he was motivated by white supremacist material he encountered while addicted to social media. The families contend these companies are liable because they intentionally designed an addictive algorithm that destroyed his mental health while proactively steering him to pro-violence content. “The social media companies had a role in causing the crime,” attorney Jennifer Bennett argued. “Heavy social media usage goes hand-in-hand with mass shootings.” Meta attorney Eric Shumsky said the entire argument boiled down to an attempt to sue over the actual content the shooter saw, a type of claim his company is protected against. “If the addiction were to cooking tutorials or cat videos or anything else, it would be an absolutely incoherent theory of liability,” Shumsky said. Judges on the seven-person court panel acknowledged the possibility of significant repercussions no matter how they rule. “Let’s say I can’t function, I can’t work anymore, because of my addiction to social media,” Judge Michael Garcia said while questioning the plaintiffs about how far reaching lawsuits might be under their theory. “It’s addictive, I can’t deal with people, I stay home, I can’t work.” “That is a viable claim,” Bennett said. “The evidence is very strong that the social media companies made a product to have this effect.” While questioning Meta, Chief Judge Rowan Wilson raised the possibility of troubling precedents if the court supports the idea of widespread immunity for app creators. “I use AI to, let’s say, ‘design me an app to create the most harm possible to teenagers,’” Wilson said. “It’s my intent to create an app that selects content designed to destroy the mental health of teenagers … Am I liable?” — Bill Mahoney EYES ON AI: Gov. Kathy Hochul chided the federal government today for not doing enough to address concerns about the existential threats artificial intelligence potentially poses. “Understandably, Americans are concerned, as am I,” Hochul told reporters after an event Tuesday in Manhattan. “We have an obligation to ensure that technological progress does not come at our own peril. So while Washington refuses to act, here in New York, we're stepping up.” Hochul pointed to the landmark RAISE Act , which goes into effect in January, and a one-year data center moratorium, which she issued in July, as evidence that New York is acting aggressively. Her administration earlier today rolled out a framework for communities that want to host a data center to minimize detrimental effects on the area. The governor added that she’ll find “additional actions that we can take at the state level to lead the way in the absence of leadership from Washington” — though she did not specify what that looks like. While some in Washington are eager to implement restrictions to slow down AI, President Donald Trump has tried to shut down those efforts , calling the AI dooming a “HOAX.” Hochul said she hasn’t had conversations with legislators in recent days regarding AI. — Madison Fernandez FROM CITY HALL TO ENFORCE OR NOT TO ENFORCE — THAT’S THE QUESTION: Mamdani wouldn’t commit today to ordering the NYPD to step up enforcement of traffic violations in New York City — because he’s focused on “behavioral change,” not punishment. The NYPD’s rate of issuing tickets to drivers who speed, blow through red lights, block bike lanes or otherwise break traffic laws remains far below pre-pandemic levels. And transit advocates, including left-leaning allies of Mamdani , say the police department must get back to issuing more violations, arguing that it’s critical to keeping city streets safe. This afternoon, though, Mamdani declined repeatedly to say whether he will deliver such marching orders to the NYPD and suggested enforcement isn’t a key priority for him. “Our goal here is not going to be measured in terms of the number of tickets that are issued or the violations, but rather behavioral change, and the NYPD is a partner in delivering that change,” Mamdani said, speaking at a press conference in Brooklyn held to unveil his new street safety plan , which contains ambitious proposals but is light on many implementation details. How does the city change behaviors without stepping up enforcement, though? In response to that question, Mamdani suggested the answer could lie in developing more protected bus and bike lanes and otherwise redesigning streets to make them safer for pedestrians. At the same time, Mamdani said he’s committed to “a continued partnership with the PD to use those tools of ticketing when any violation is present.” “We’re going to be taking a hard look at how best we can change behavior that we’re seeing in violation of street safety laws, and then utilize that. That includes the PD,” he said. The mayor’s comments came after Streetsblog reported the NYPD has shifted its traffic violation strategy to prioritize enforcement against scofflaws on e-bikes and other micromobility vehicles. That shift comes in spite of the fact that car drivers account for the vast majority of crashes and traffic deaths in the city, data shows. — Chris Sommerfeldt   FOILED ATTEMPT: The Manhattan Institute, a conservative think tank, is suing the Mamdani administration over its handling of Freedom of Information Law requests. The think tank has been seeking records related to meetings between foreign dignitaries and Ana María Archila, commissioner of the Mayor’s Office of International Affairs. Archila has faced criticism for attempting to meet with an Iranian diplomat amid that country’s war with the U.S. While the Adams administration provided tailored estimates for FOIL requests (but by no means fulfilled them in a timely manner), the institute found Mamdani’s City Hall team began giving out blanket six-month timetables for fulfilling requests. “City Hall has turned FOIL into a six-month waiting room for everyone,” Manhattan Institute City Policy Analyst Santiago Vidal Calvo and General Counsel Cameron Macdonald wrote in explaining their suit , which was filed in Manhattan Supreme Court. “That is why we are suing.” The city did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. — Joe Anuta SCREENS IN SCHOOLS: The New York City public school system banned unfettered access to YouTube on school-issued devices for the current school year, the Department of Education revealed Tuesday. The ban — which went into effect last week, ahead of the first day of school — comes amid calls from City Council members to limit the use of YouTube, personal devices and AI in the classroom. “We heard everyone loud and clear,” DOE official Scott Strickland said at a Council hearing today. “As of Wednesday night at 5 p.m., we filtered YouTube out of all student devices. They shouldn’t be able to access it either on a Chromebook or an iPad both at school and at home.” Council member Shekar Krishnan, who chairs the Council’s Oversight and Investigations Committee and was co-leading Tuesday’s hearing, said he was “very glad to hear” of the YouTube ban. Educational videos embedded into Google Classroom for specific lessons will be exempt from the ban. Earlier this month, Mamdani announced a year-long AI moratorium for students in grades 2-K through eighth grade. Hochul and lawmakers in Albany also rolled out a full-day “bell-to-bell” restriction on cellphone use during the school day last school year. Ahead of this afternoon’s hearing, Krishnan and Council member Eric Dinowitz, who chairs the Education Committee, held a rally railing against screen-heavy classroom instruction and calling, among other things, for a YouTube ban. “We will not let the greed of big technology companies get in the way of our children's future and their education," Krishnan said at the rally. — Molly Reinmann IN OTHER NEWS — DECLASSIFIED DOCS: Trump said he’d consider releasing classified documents related to 9/11 after victims’ families pleaded for clarity on Saudi Arabia’s involvement. ( NY Post ) — TIED UP: Long Island Democratic House candidate Christopher Gallant acknowledged he posed in bondage gear for an ad campaign over a decade ago. ( The New York Times ) — ICE ARRESTS: Police in the Westchester village of Port Chester have turned over more people with no criminal record to ICE than other local law enforcement agencies, despite assertions the police department would not cooperate with ICE. articles.body: Texas Republicans were already fretting about slipping support with voters of color. Then Bo French got on X. The Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner posted a photo of a crowd of University of Texas football fans, most of them people of color, saying , “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” The Sunday morning comments, which appeared to target South Asian students, sent Lone Star Republicans into a frenzy, worried about the impact the rhetoric could have on GOP candidates up and down the ballot, including Attorney General Ken Paxton’s high-profile Senate race and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s reelection fight. A number of Republican lawmakers, including some in tough races, quickly denounced the post as racist, as others squirmed with carefully worded statements. And GOP operatives winced at the potential electoral backlash — in a year that’s already looking tougher-than-normal for a party that has dominated the state for decades. Still, no one explicitly called for him to drop out of the race. “His post on social media is profoundly unhelpful if his goal is to see Republicans win statewide races in a tough political environment in 50 days,” said Matt Mackowiak, an Austin-based GOP consultant who advised Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) unsuccessful primary campaign against Paxton. Cornyn condemned the post , asking whether other GOP officials would “condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized.” Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas), who is facing a tough reelection fight in a Hispanic-majority district, told POLITICO in a statement she’s willing to “condemn racism” wherever it comes from. "All I see in that photograph is a group of kids celebrating a Longhorns win. What can be more Texan than that?” De La Cruz said, before taking a shot at her Democratic opponent, Bobby Pulido, for his past racial comments . And Karl Rove, a longtime adviser to former President George W. Bush, called French a “bigot” at a private lunch event and said he’s voting for French’s Democratic opponent, The Texas Tribune reported . Meanwhile, state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat running against French, said he had his best fundraising day of the cycle after French’s post. French didn’t respond to requests for comment. He repeatedly stood by his comments since Sunday morning. During a local radio appearance Monday, he said he didn’t have any personal animosity against the students at the football game, but said that it is “not racist to point out that we should be favoring Texans over foreigners” and that his fellow Republicans are afraid of being called racist . The divide emerging among Texas Republicans over the social media post — and Democrats’ eagerness to capitalize on it — show just how precarious the party finds its position this cycle. Texas Republicans were already worrying about losing support from Hispanic and other minority voters amid a tough economic environment and President Donald Trump’s unpopular immigration agenda. They need to hold onto or improve the incremental gains they made over previous cycles with voters of color in a fast-changing state where non-Hispanic white people now only make up 37% of the population. The stakes are high this cycle: Most polls show Paxton slightly trailing in a Senate race that could determine control of the upper chamber; Abbott appears to be in the toughest of his four election fights; and the state is home to several key House races. “I don’t think [French’s post] independently and universally sours voter sentiment. But it contributes to GOP declining numbers with Hispanic voters particularly in the South Texas congressional races which we hope to win,” said Alfredo Rodriguez, a Dallas-based Republican strategist, who called on French to “stop the petty political theatrics.” The blast radius of French’s posts was wide enough to garner carefully worded responses from the top of the ticket. Abbott said in a Sunday statement that French’s post “is not my message,” before noting unity “doesn’t mean that Texas cannot also lead in having the toughest immigration laws of any state in America and freezing H1B visas at our universities.” Two of the students in the photo told the Dallas Morning News that they’re U.S. citizens . Most UT students are Texans — state law requires that 90% of each freshman class come from in-state — and there is no evidence that the students in the photo French posted are foreigners. Some Republicans weren’t thrilled about Abbott’s response. “This had nothing to do with illegal immigrants,” said Anang Mittal, an Indian American national GOP strategist, of Abbott’s comments. “These were students at a college game. They're not H-1B. If they're students, they're on a student visa. … It's pretty damn disgusting of Greg Abbott to say, ‘I condemn racism, but also, like, we're keeping all the Indians out.’ That's essentially what that tweet read to me.” Democrat James Talarico called Paxton out on social media, asking if he would follow Cornyn’s lead in denouncing French’s post. The GOP nominee replied that he condemns “racism in all its forms” — and then claimed Talarico had a “history of dividing Texans by race.” Spokespeople for Paxton and Abbott did not respond to requests for comment. Other Republicans were less willing to fully denounce French’s comments. “I don't really know the guy. I heard he said some not so pleasant things,” said Rep. Troy Nehls (R-Texas), who said he hadn’t seen the posts — but launched into a criticism of immigration nonetheless. “I am concerned about the number of people living in this country, and we don't even know who they really are,” he said. ”Shut the border down for 10 years, and then let's try to figure out who we got in this country because we don't even know." Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.), who campaigned with Talarico in Houston on Sunday, said French’s posts came up in conversations with every Asian American voter he met. “Everyone was talking about it,” Kim said. “Every single Asian American that I was with yesterday raised this with me. They were saying this is an example of, ‘Not only are they not courting us or engaging with us, but they’re actively demonizing us, actively being xenophobic and racist towards us.’ We need leaders that stand up against this.” The political damage could also extend — potentially for years — to Texas’ small but growing Indian American population, the demographic group French appeared to target in his posts. Both Dallas and Houston have significant Indian American populations. In 2019, an event at a Houston stadium headlined by Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi drew over 50,000 attendees. French’s comments could alienate those same voters, said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican consultant in Austin. “He just irritated a bunch of people, many of whom could be supporters and could be Republicans,” said Steinhauser, a University of Texas graduate. “I'd be willing to bet a lot of those kids that he was posting a photo of are probably, you know, their parents might be Republicans, or they might be Republicans, or conservatives, or independent-leaning conservatives.” If French is elected, he would sit on a commission that regulates Texas’ powerful oil, gas and mining industries — which has little to do with immigration or social issues. But French, a longtime provocateur in Texas political circles, has a history of incendiary statements. Just last year, Republicans were calling on French to resign as chair of the Tarrant County Republican Party after he published an online poll asking whether Muslims or Jews were “the bigger threat to America.” He deleted the post and said he regretted it, adding “antisemitism has no place in the Republican Party.” This spring, he unseated a well-financed Republican incumbent for Texas Railroad Commission. French isn’t the only politician in Texas who has made singling out Muslims part of his political brand. Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick has made “preventing Shariah law in Texas” one of his legislative priorities. Patrick didn’t respond to a request for comment. Abbott, Paxton and Cornyn have all called for investigations and other government action to stop development of a commercial and residential development being built by the East Plano Islamic Center, a mosque outside Dallas . And just last month, Abbott threatened to withhold funding from Dallas Fort Worth International Airport to block plans for ritual washing facilities for Muslim travelers in the airport’s terminals. There’s little difference between French’s attacks and the other politicians’ actions, said Yasir Qadhi, an Islamic scholar at the Islamic center.“It is the same mindset,” he said in an interview. “What we're witnessing is really an unprecedented and increasingly brazen form of racism. It's unfiltered, it's unapologetic, it's even stripped of even the pretense of political correctness. You know, this is a type of racism we've never seen in our lifetimes.” When French unleashed a string of inflammatory social media posts in 2025, several GOP officeholders — including Patrick, the lieutenant governor — called on him to resign as county GOP chair. But Republicans now refuse to tell French to drop out now “because that might mean that there would be a Democrat elected statewide,” said Glen Whitley, a Republican former Tarrant County judge. “That's the bottom line.” “That's part of my frustration with the Republican Party altogether: They talk about being Christian, but they get up every morning to talk about who they hate,” said Whitley, who still identifies as Republican but endorsed Talarico for Senate. Joey Fox contributed to this report.
articles.headline: Texas Republicans are scrambling after Bo French’s outburst

articles.body: NEW YORK — A state lawmaker who gained national attention for his opposition to unchecked AI during a failed campaign for Congress this year is launching a $30 million effort to unite Democrats around regulating the technology, according to the organization’s new website. New York Assemblymember Alex Bores is unveiling the organization — called “Who Decides” — on Tuesday to “build the winning Democratic answer to AI,” according to a website that was publicly available Monday night. “Who Decides’ goal is that by 2028, Democratic candidates from the top of the ticket on down run with a common AI safety agenda,” reads an announcement on the site dated Tuesday . “That means addressing the harms people already see and the broader danger that increasingly powerful and out-of-control systems could destabilize our economy, our democracy, and our safety.” It was not immediately clear whether Who Decides would be organized as a federal super PAC, 501(c)(4) nonprofit or other type of group. The website has a “donate” link that redirects to a webpage hosted by “Give Butter,” an organization focused on helping nonprofits fundraise. The announcement said the group would reject “corporate money or contributions from senior executives at frontier AI companies.” Bores did not immediately respond to questions about the organization Monday night, including whether Bores, a sitting state lawmaker, personally fundraised for the group while holding public office. He is launching the organization with his former chief of staff, Anna Myers, the website says. The apparent launch of Who Decides comes at a moment when the quickly-advancing technology has become a major political issue. Last week, a former Anthropic researcher issued a dire warning that artificial intelligence has a chance of bringing about the end of humanity. The concerns from the researcher, Jacob Coxon, who also worked for OpenAI, were followed up by calls from the leaders of Anthropic and OpenAI, along with Elon Musk, to regulate the industry and slow development to build more guardrails. Politicians have scrambled to respond, with both parties trying to coalesce around a policy agenda — and political message — on the rapidly evolving issue. Former President Barack Obama called last week for Democrats to focus on AI , and prominent party strategists from across the ideological spectrum gathered to begin mapping out a strategy . President Donald Trump rejected recent calls from Republicans and Democrats to quickly regulate the industry in a spate of Monday social media posts . “We don’t let five people write the laws for hundreds of millions of Americans,” Bores says in the launch announcement on the website, an apparent reference to the top executives in the AI industry. “There is no reason to let them write the rules for AI.” The group says on the site it will focus on 11 states that it says will be key to the 2028 presidential primary and general election: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, Virginia, Arizona, Georgia, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. It says it will conduct quarterly national and state polls, host national conferences and partner with local groups in the states. Earlier this year, Bores lost the primary for retiring Manhattan Democratic Rep. Jerry Nadler’s seat. His campaign largely centered on a push to regulate artificial intelligence following his work to pass the RAISE Act in the state Legislature, which aimed to enact safeguards for the technology. His campaign attracted a combined $21 million from super PACs backed by dueling factions of the AI community, which spent both in support and opposition of him. Democratic Assemblymember Micah Lasher ultimately won the primary and is all but assured to win in November in the deep-blue seat. “The lesson Bores and Myers took from those fights was that confronting the AI industry is fertile political ground and that public demand for answers on AI policy exists but remains scattered,” the website said, referencing his congressional campaign. “What’s missing is a coalition capable of turning that energy into a governing consensus before the technology, the economic dislocation, and the partisan battle lines harden.”
articles.headline: Alex Bores launches $30 million effort to unify Dems on AI

articles.body: ICE TO SEE YOU: Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office is advising local governments that zoning and state environmental laws can stymie Immigration and Customs Enforcement from building or expanding detention facilities in their communities. Those legal barriers — spelled out in a letter sent today by Hochul to local government leaders — represent the latest effort by her administration to halt ICE’s efforts in New York. “We need localities focused on keeping our communities safe, which depends upon the efforts of local law enforcement, civil servants, and regulators,” Hochul wrote in the letter, which was exclusively obtained by Playbook. “While my administration will continue to demand answers and transparency from federal immigration authorities, should you become aware of these projects, my office is ready to partner with you to determine any appropriate next steps to protect our local communities.” The missive is a new front in Hochul’s broader push to erect roadblocks against President Donald Trump’s sweeping deportation campaign — which includes a push to build or convert facilities in parts of New York. New York lawmakers and Hochul agreed in May to a package of sweeping measures meant to limit Trump’s immigration enforcement. Included in those measures were provisions that required expanded public notice — including holding at least two hearings — for the expansion or construction of an immigration detention facility. The law also prohibits local governments from providing financial benefits meant to offset the cost of a facility. Hochul’s Republican critics have railed against the measures, which were first proposed during the aggressive deportation crackdown in Minnesota, which left two U.S. citizens dead. Broome County Sheriff Fred Akshar is set to testify Tuesday to the House Judiciary Committee in Washington on “the continuing tragedy of sanctuary laws.” Akshar’s office did not immediately return a message seeking comment. Local government officials have already sounded an alarm this year over ICE’s apparent efforts to expand the agency’s detention capacity by leasing or expanding sites in Batavia, Newburgh and Rochester. Hochul wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin earlier this summer requesting more information on ICE’s New York plans. Last month her administration got a reply. An ICE official wrote to the governor that the agency has “not directed the establishment of a detention facility” in Rochester. In Batavia, ICE is “in the early stages” of weighing a bedspace and usage expansion at a site. And in the Hudson Valley, the agency confirmed that “an acquisition [is] underway to identify a new facility to lease through the General Services Administration” that would house its investigations, enforcement and removal operations. Details were scant in the letter, but the response is the first time the federal government has formally laid out any of its plans for ICE expansion in New York to state officials. On Monday in New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and state Attorney General Letitia James offered some of their own push back: two lawsuits seeking to stop the Trump administration from making it harder for immigrants lawfully in the U.S. to change their status. The suits target a federal rule change set to take effect Friday. The change would give immigration agents more leeway to deny green cards or visas to lawful immigrants on the basis of being a “public charge” — someone who’s using social safety net programs. The rule change would allow agents to factor in the use of Medicaid or food assistance into their decision making. The Trump administration has said the rule is necessary to ensure the country is not authorizing immigrants who drain public resources. Mamdani countered that, rather than saving the U.S. money, the change will force immigrants to forgo routine medical care, increasing the likelihood of medical emergencies. “None of this is abstract,” Mamdani said. “People could die as a result of these changes.” James said the administration’s rule change is overly broad and flies in the face of more than 100 years of legal precedent. “This public charge rule goes back to 1822, where Congress basically said that it only applies to individuals who cannot support themselves, not individuals who apply every now and then for public assistance because they fall on hard times,” she said. — Nick Reisman and Joe Anuta From the Capitol REGENTS EXAM PHASE-OUT COMING: The high school class of 2027 will be the final one required to pass the state Regents exams to graduate. The state Board of Regents authorized the Education Department today to move forward with the next phase of the “New York Inspires” program. As part of that program, the board voted last year to adopt a framework that lets students demonstrate proficiency through other measures like projects or coursework. That framework will replace the Regents exam. While the Regents will remain as an option, it will no longer be a requirement for high school graduation, beginning with students graduating in 2028, education officials said during the board’s monthly meeting today. “For years, we looked at what elite private schools provide for their students and they do not worry about the Regents exam,” State Education Commissioner Betty Rosa said. “They don’t even worry when you apply to colleges that it’s on their transcript.” The department said it plans to advance the regulation changes to the board by February 2027 so it can implement the changes in the 2027-28 school year. The board unanimously passed a resolution to that effect today. Districts will have to develop strategies for assessment that draw on multiple sources of evidence, including classroom performance, student work and state assessments. Some Regents board members sought more clarity on resources to support families. “What I did not hear was what resources, what tools do we have for parents and students who are in this purgatory period?” said Regents member Hasoni Pratts, a New York City public school parent. The news comes as the state grapples with abysmal performance on this year’s reading exams — despite New York spending more per pupil than any other state in the country. Experts and advocates have been questioning what those results say about student learning, and precisely what led to those fluctuations. — Madina Touré FROM CITY HALL DEEPFAKE CRACKDOWN: Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg announced today that his office seized control of a dozen domains used to create, disseminate and sell AI deepfake porn. The sites in question featured AI-generated images and videos of roughly 1,200 individuals — primarily women and celebrities — engaging in sexually explicit activity. “These horrific violations of privacy follow victims into their careers and personal lives, and take an immense toll on their emotional and mental well-being,” Bragg said. “We were able to seize these domains because a brave survivor stepped forward. And while victims of these sites are largely celebrities, we know that anyone can be a victim of these crimes, particularly in domestic violence cases.” New York penal law prohibits the dissemination of pornography without a subject’s consent, and violations are punishable by up to a year in prison. That statute was updated in 2023 to explicitly prohibit AI-generated porn. Bragg’s announcement comes as lawmakers in Albany and Washington grapple with the looming threat of artificial intelligence. But Bragg declined to comment on the potential role of the Manhattan DA’s office in working towards larger scale AI regulation. “This is a crime in New York State,” he said, referring to the circulation of deepfake pornography. “We don't have to talk about regulation, legislation. This is a crime now.” — Molly Reinmann FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL 2028 VISION: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is leaning into the speculation swirling around her 2028 aspirations. “In some ways, I understand the interest. But I wanted to write to you today to be direct about what I’m focused on,” Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a fundraising email . “Frankly, I could not care less about titles or positions for myself. That’s not why I got into this work. What matters to me is changing this country so that it finally works for all of us, and that’s why my focus is on the decision working people around the country will make in the next 50 days.” She added that her political operation is “mobilizing resources, not just to get me re-elected or build for a future campaign, but most importantly to win the midterms and take back the majority.” Ocasio-Cortez, who’s been active on the trail boosting down-ballot candidates, has kept the door open for either a Senate run or a presidential bid in 2028 — though some progressives are urging her to aim for the White House . Any clarity on her 2028 decision before this coming Election Day seems unlikely, though — especially given how “concerned” she says she is “by how some in our party are talking” about the midterms. “There is a narrative taking hold in Washington that the Republicans are already cooked,” her email continued. “That kind of complacency is how we grasp defeat from the jaws of victory. … All of this is why I am not spending this fall thinking about myself. I am spending it working my butt off to deliver a majority in the House and the Senate.” — Madison Fernandez A DIFFERENT LAUDER GIVES: Estee Lauder Chair William Lauder gave $500,000 to the super PAC backing Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman. Lauder’s contribution comes after his uncle, prolific GOP donor Ronald Lauder, ceased his political giving this year . Ronald Lauder was the principal backer of a super PAC aiding Republican Lee Zeldin’s 2022 bid against Hochul. William Lauder wasn’t the only deep-pocketed titan to donate to the Blakeman PAC recently. Home Depot founder Ken Langone, a GOP megadonor who once led Republicans for Cuomo, gave $50,000. — Nick Reisman  IN OTHER NEWS — STALLED SECURITY: More than eight months into his term, Mamdani is still waiting on federal security clearance. ( Gothamist ) — LEGIONELLA LOCATIONS: A Yankee Stadium cooling tower tested positive for the bacteria that can cause Legionnaires’ disease, according to the New York City Health Department. ( Daily News ) — SIGN LANGUAGE: A PAC funded by Knicks owner James Dolan launched a $250,000 billboard campaign backing Blakeman and blaming Hochul for an exodus from the state. articles.body: Bo French, the GOP nominee for a spot on the Texas Railroad Commission, doubled down on Monday on a xenophobic post that disparaged Asian American students at the University of Texas after receiving blowback from fellow Republicans over the weekend. On X, French was quick to turn his viral post, which had received more than 35 million views as of Monday afternoon, into a fundraising pledge , calling the criticism he has received an attack from “the radical left and their allies.” He also stood by his post in an appearance on the conservative radio broadcast "The Mark Davis Show" on Monday. “The radical left, you know, they want to make everything about race,” he said on the show. “Of course, there are some people in our party who are uncomfortable talking about those things because it scares them.” The social media firestorm started after French posted a photo on X on Sunday of UT students celebrating in the crowd and wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” The post drew swift rebukes from Democrats and some Texas Republicans, including outgoing Sen. John Cornyn — who called on other Republican officials to “condemn the intolerance and racism” — as well as several state lawmakers. During his radio appearance, French said his social media post is a criticism of admissions and hiring policies at UT, the state’s public flagship, that he said discriminated against Texas residents. “It’s not racist to point out that we should be favoring Texans over foreigners,” French said. There's no indication that the students French targeted are foreigners. Most of UT’s student body is made up of Texans. According to state law, Texas high school students in the top 5% of their class are automatically admitted to UT, and around 80% of the student body is from the state. He also took a shot at Cornyn and other Republicans who condemned him, saying many were from the establishment wing of the party that opposed him in the GOP primary. “What is he doing to help elect [Ken] Paxton? So we have to ask those questions,” he said. “I just think we should be prioritizing our Republican platform, which, by the way, is an America First platform, which prioritizes Americans.” French, who is running for a seat on the influential statewide body that regulates its oil and gas industry, has a history of making controversial statements. Earlier this year, he suggested Republicans should fear Islam and advocated for deporting 100 million people.
articles.headline: Texas GOP candidate stands by xenophobic comments following backlash

articles.body: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has a simmering Latino revolt on his hands. Quelling it could come down to Texas. A group of Latino Democratic officials — including operatives and local and congressional leaders — are pushing Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association, to pounce on late-breaking momentum in the Texas gubernatorial race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is vying to unseat incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott. The effort to get Beshear to expand the map comes as the DGA eyes several swing states — like Michigan, Arizona, Georgia or Nevada — where the party is focused on keeping or flipping governors’ mansions. But underlying it all is the Democratic Party’s fight to staunch the hemorrhaging of Latino voters from their ranks, and Texas sits at the center of their losses. “One takeaway from 2024 is that Democrats writ large need to be a whole lot more bold when it comes to their approach, their strategy, their thinking,” said Sergio Gonzalez, one of the operatives involved in the effort to recruit DGA’s support who’s working with Latino candidates across the country. “How do [Democrats] build the coalition that it's going to take for them to ultimately be successful? Gina is very much a part of that task.” The Latino operatives and lawmakers made their case in a letter earlier this month asking the DGA to drop $10 million on Hinojosa’s race, pointing to multiple polls that put the state representative within striking distance of Abbott. An investment from the DGA, they argued , could help make inroads with Latino voters and give Democrats what’s proved to be an elusive statewide victory in deep-red Texas. Instead, the Latino coalition behind the letter said they got snubbed. The DGA’s response to the letter, shared with the Latino organizers last Sunday and viewed by POLITICO, called Hinojosa an “outstanding candidate running a strong campaign,” and touted the work it’s already done investing in campaign staff and research in coordination with the campaign. But the Latino leaders were ultimately disappointed by a lack of commitment from the DGA to financially boost Hinojosa. “We would be grateful for your help in raising the resources necessary to expand the map and go big in Texas,” the DGA wrote in its response. “We welcome your fundraising collaboration to support Gina’s campaign.” The group said that after receiving the DGA’s response, they reached out to the organization and requested a meeting with Beshear, but they have not heard back. The DGA, however, says it’s not taking anything off the table. “The DGA is excited to be supporting Gina Hinojosa’s campaign for governor of Texas and has been working directly with her team since she’s launched,” DGA communications director Sam Newton said in a statement to POLITICO. “We’ve been in touch and have made clear we look forward to setting up a meeting to find a productive path forward.” The DGA also has not ruled out investing in Hinojosa’s race, the organization told POLITICO. “Gina Hinojosa is a great candidate and running a great campaign,” Beshear told POLITICO in a statement. “We are currently investing by paying expenses and recently providing staff. My goal as chair of the DGA this year is to win as many races as we can and that's exactly what we're doing by going on offense and expanding the map.” Hinojosa said the DGA has been “a great partner since the beginning,” and that her campaign has a “good working relationship” with them. Asked if she believes they’ll spend for her in the final stretch, she said, “I sure hope they do.” While Texas is a central focus of the fight Democrats and Republicans are waging to win the Latino vote, it’s states like Arizona and Nevada that have more competitive governor’s races — and are likely to showcase the influence of Latino voters in 2028. The DGA has made seven-figure investments in those states, running Spanish-language ads since May in Arizona. In their conference last week, Beshear announced a new “expand the map” fund to collect more resources to flip more seats, which could help races like Texas. But the lack of assurances on whether the DGA will step in with a financial salve for Hinojosa has been cold comfort for the Latinos backing her. The result is what operatives called a “sweeping frustration” among their ranks at what they view as “dismissiveness” from the DGA. “In just over a month, people will cast their first ballots in Texas. It's not like we have tons of time to iron this out,” said Gonzalez, who helped organize the letter to the DGA. Hinojosa’s race is rated likely Republican , and she is facing a significant fundraising disadvantage to Abbott. Texas is flooded with media markets among the most expensive in the country. Yet the operatives argue Hinojosa presents one of the best Democratic opportunities in the state in years. And they believe her campaign could get a boost from voters turning out for Democrat James Talarico in the Senate race, as well as down-ballot candidates with high name identification like Bobby Pulido. “What is especially egregious in this particular situation is that she was coming from behind,” Jess Rocketto, another Latino operative working closely with Latino candidates who helped coordinate the letter, told POLITICO. “Now that she has come up from behind, they still don't want to invest. What is the DGA for in that case?” And the operatives say the frustrations in Texas could ultimately land hardest on Beshear, who’s built a national profile as a Democrat able to flip a red-state governor’s seat held by an incumbent. He’s also been actively courting the Latino vote, collaborating frequently with top Latino creators like Carlos Eduardo Espina . “We would really think, just to be honest with you, that Governor Beshear would understand this, especially given that he has presidential aspirations,” Gonzalez said. “It's very important that he understand this.” Another Latino operative who signed the letter, granted anonymity to speak candidly, argued Beshear will need these same Latinos if he moves to build a coalition for 2028. “He's not being smart about his politics,” they said. And in Texas, the operative warned that a failure to invest in Hinojosa now could not only make her uphill battle even harder, but it could also make it “next to impossible” to recruit a strong Latino candidate in the future. “If they can't show that they’re showing up for their people, Texas is written off for Democrats for a generation,” they said. articles.body: El dia de la cavalcada de la Mercè 2026 és un dels plats forts del programa de la Festa Major de Barcelona . La desfilada, un clàssic de les festes, tornarà a omplir els carrers del centre de la ciutat de gegants , bèsties , capgrossos i molta música . Et detallem tot el que has de saber de la cavalcada de la Mercè 2026 , que es farà el dijous 24 de setembre . També t’expliquem el recorregut i l’ horari de la desfilada de gegants . També et pot interessar Gegants per la Mercè 2026: On i quan veure’n? Toc d’inici, cercavila i cavalcada amb els horaris Eva Vial Sílvia Carbonell 3 minuts de lectura Cavalcada de la Mercè 2026: recorregut La cavalcada de la Mercè arrencarà a les 18 h del dijous 24 de setembre , a la plaça de Catalunya i recorrerà els carrers Fontanella, via Laietana i Jaume I. Finalment, la desfilada arribarà a la plaça de Sant Jaume i les colles entraran a l’Ajuntament de Barcelona amb els balls dels Capgrossos Macers, de l’Àliga i dels Gegants de la Ciutat. També et pot interessar Concerts de la Mercè 2026: Cartell complet per dies, hores i escenaris Núria Dias 5 minuts de lectura Horari i on veure la cavalcada de la Mercè Si no et vols perdre cap detall de la Cavalcada de la Mercè 2026 , pots seguir-la des de qualsevol dels punts del recorregut. Recorda que la desfilada començarà a les 18 h a la plaça de Catalunya i arribarà a la plaça de Sant Jaume a les 19 h, on finalitzarà el recorregut cap a les 21 h , amb l’entrada de tots els participants a l’Ajuntament. L’acte més constant i vistós La desfilada de la Mercè és l’acte de la festa major que, des dels inicis del segle passat, ha estat més constant i vistós. Els gegants són l’eix central d’aquest esdeveniment, organitzat per la coordinadora de Colles Geganteres de Barcelona, que es fa el dijous 24 de setembre . A la Cavalcada d’enguany, a més, segurament descobrireu entre els grups locals de cultura popular alguns elements xinesos que han arribat des de Shanghai, la ciutat convidada. articles.body: (ACN/Redacció) El director de la Representació de la Comissió Europea (CE) a Espanya, Daniel Calleja , creu que Barcelona “té una oportunitat extraordinària” amb la intel·ligència artificial (IA). “Barcelona té una sèrie d’actius que poden ser molt útils si s’orienten a donar més competitivitat i facilitar l’accés a les empreses”, va dir en unes declaracions al Forward Tech Summit . Es tracta del primer congrés sobre IA impulsat per Foment del Treball , que va exhaurir les entrades i que es va organitzar amb la intenció que les pimes tinguin accés als experts en la matèria, tant amb conferències com amb assessorament personalitzat, perquè apostin més i millor per aquesta tecnologia, que està liderada pels Estats Units i la Xina . També et pot interessar Barcelona defensa apostar per la IA “sense tancar els ulls als debats” Helena Molist Sancho 2 minuts de lectura Les grans empreses fan servir la IA el triple Segons Calleja, hi ha una bretxa rellevant entre pimes i grans companyies a l’hora de fer servir la IA. En concret, situa en el 19 % l’ús entre les petites i mitjanes empreses , un percentatge que s’enfila fins al 57 % en les grans companyies, és a dir, el triple. En aquest sentit, opina que cal “alfabetització” perquè les pimes, que formen la majoria del teixit empresarial de Catalunya, estiguin “més ben formades en tot el que implica la IA”. També creu que els cal més finançament. “Les pimes necessiten ajudes per poder invertir”, diu. Segons Calleja, que fa més de 30 anys que es dedica a les polítiques de la UE, la IA pot aportar “molta més productivitat i competitivitat ” i cal continuar desenvolupant-la perquè farà el teixit empresarial “més eficient”. També et pot interessar El Nobel Philippe Aghion defensa polítiques públiques per fer front a l’impacte laboral de la IA Redacció 2 minuts de lectura Cristian Canton, director del Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) Barcelona, un dels pols de la IA a Europa En ple debat sobre l’avenç d’aquesta tecnologia, l’alt càrrec europeu diu que “no s’ha de tenir por” i defensa que “les solucions de laboratori es traslladin a l’economia real”. Per la seva banda, el director associat del Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC), Cristian Canton, va afirmar al mateix congrés que la capital catalana està “molt ben situada dins l’ecosistema europeu” de la IA. Canton també va afirmar que Barcelona és un dels pols de la IA a Europa. “N’hem de parlar més, hem d’aprofundir-hi perquè tothom sigui conscient de l’esforç que s’està fent”, opina l’expert, que durant anys ha treballat als Estats Units. “Moltes vegades hi ha diners públics que s’han invertit a fer models d’IA, per tant, realment són diners que estan revertint un altre cop en la societat”, afegeix, alhora que cita projectes desenvolupats al BSC com l’AINA i l’ALIA, de codi obert per a les empreses. “El món de la IA està evolucionant a una velocitat extrema”, afirma. És per aquest motiu que aposta per “regular més ràpid” i deixar clar a les empreses “on estan les línies vermelles, què es pot fer i què no es pot fer, abans de tenir un incident”. “Ara mateix és un tema candent i és un tema en què hem de posar tots els esforços”, adverteix dies després que el cofundador d’Anthropic, Dario Amodei , hagi demanat que se n’alenteixi el desenvolupament. “S’ha de créixer de manera ordenada, de manera conscient, i no simplement anar a provar qualsevol cosa que funcioni i després ja es corregirà”, afirma. “Més val fer-ho bé a la primera i després no haver-ho de corregir”, sentencia. articles.body: (ACN) DWS, la gestora d’actius del grup Deutsche Bank, ha posat a la venda el centre comercial Diagonal Mar de Barcelona i busca obtenir-ne més de 500 milions d’euros , segons ha avançat aquest dimecres El Periódico i ha pogut confirmar l’ACN de fonts del mercat immobiliari. L’operació situa al mercat un dels principals actius comercials de la capital catalana, ubicat al districte de Sant Martí. DWS ha encarregat a les consultores immobiliàries CBRE i JLL l’assessorament en el procés de venda del centre, que té uns 90.000 metres quadrats de superfície comercial. També et pot interessar Leo Messi compra les galeries Wagner per 11,5 milions d’euros Ester Magdaleno 1 minut de lectura 25 anys d’activitat comercial El centre comercial es va inaugurar el 2001 i surt a la venda vuit anys després de sotmetre’s a una reforma per canviar d’imatge . Aleshores va guanyar espai per a zona comercial i d’oferta gastronòmica, es van reduir les sales de cinema i es va eliminar la pista de bitlles per poder acollir els comerços nous.

articles.body: El correfoc de les Festes de la Mercè 2026 és una de les celebracions més esperades i multitudinàries de la Festa Major de Barcelona i, concretament, de la cultura popular . Els diables de les colles de tota la ciutat i les moltes bèsties de foc ballaran pels carrers i els convertiran en un mar d’espurnes, entre explosions i ensurts. Aquí tens una guia ràpida per descobrir tot el que has de saber sobre el correfoc de la Mercè 2026 , amb el recorregut , el dia i l’ hora de l’espectacle de focs de les festes. També et pot interessar La Mercè 2026 a Barcelona: Programa en PDF, concerts, Piromusical i portes obertes de la festa major Neus Valls Núria Dias Sílvia Carbonell 9 minuts de lectura Correfoc de la Mercè 2026: on i quan se celebra? El correfoc de la Mercè es farà el dissabte 26 de setembre , a les 20.30 h , al passeig de Gràcia . Començarà amb la  Ceptrotada , l’encesa conjunta dels ceptrots, forques i estendards més espectaculars de cada colla, que portaran en Llucifer, la Diablessa, el Diable Gros i la resta de personatges singulars dels grups participants. Nova porta de l’infern Una de les novetats d’aquest correfoc serà l’estrena de la porta de l’infern , la més gran de la història i que dona el tret de sortida d’aquest esdeveniment. Quan s’apagui la pirotècnia, la porta s’obrirà i en sortiran els diables, dracs i bèsties de foc. El correfoc ja haurà començat ! També et pot interessar Concerts de la Mercè 2026: Cartell complet per dies, hores i escenaris Núria Dias 5 minuts de lectura Recorregut del correfoc de la Mercè 2026 La porta de l’infern, inici del correfoc , estarà situada al passeig de Gràcia a la confluència amb el carrer de Provença . Des d’allà, les criatures diabòliques aniran ballant pel passeig fins a arribar al carrer del Consell de Cent , on finalitzarà l’acte. Es tracta del mateix recorregut que va haver-hi en l’edició de l’any passat. A banda, hi haurà el correfoc infantil , per als més petits. Eva Vial 3 minuts de lectura Recomanacions per al correfoc El correfoc de la Mercè es podrà gaudir també des de la distància, però si vols ballar sota una pluja d’espurnes, tingues present un seguit de recomanacions : Vesteix amb màniga llarga i pantalons llargs : com més coberta la pell, millor, sempre amb roba de cotó (el material sintètic es pot inflamar). Porta un mocador de cotó per tapar el coll, un barret per protegir el cap i també calçat adequat, com sabatilles esportives o de muntanya. Protegeix bé els ulls i les orelles  dels trons: unes ulleres i uns taps poden ser molt útils. Ni alcohol ni vidre : si tens set, porta líquids sense alcohol i evita els recipients de vidre, ja que si es trenquen poden representar un perill. Els infants, a distància : els infants s’ho passaran millor en el correfoc infantil, però si també aneu al correfoc, que estiguin sempre lluny de la primera fila i del foc. No llancis aigua a les persones assistents al correfoc. Si tens una emergència : si pateixes una cremada o no et trobes bé, a la zona sempre hi haurà serveis mèdics i ambulàncies preparats per atendre. correfoc merce 2024 carrers tallats Una tradició que es remunta al 1979 El correfoc de la Mercè va néixer el 1979 com a Mostra de Bèsties Fantàstiques, dins el projecte de renovació i popularització de la Festa Major de la ciutat, i ràpidament es va convertir en un fenomen multitudinari i simbòlic de la Mercè. articles.body: Segons ha admès el tinent d’alcaldia de Seguretat de Barcelona, Albert Batlle , la publicació “per error” de dades personals de membres de la Guàrdia Urbana va afectar un total de 1.245 agents del cos; és més del doble dels que s’havien dit en un primer moment. En concret, a la Gaseta Municipal de Barcelona es van publicar els noms i cognoms complets, les unitats de destinació i els torns de treball dels agents que van concórrer en processos de promoció i de mobilitat interna del cos. Batlle ho ha explicat a la Comissió de Presidència i Seguretat d’aquest mes de setembre, en una compareixença forçada per Junts i Vox . El tinent d’alcaldia ha explicat que les dades es van publicar entre el setembre del 2023 i el maig del 2026 –en 38 documents ja eliminats–, seguint “erròniament els mateixos criteris que s’utilitzen amb la resta de treballadors municipals”. Albert Batlle ha assegurat que l’ Ajuntament ja ha elaborat una instrucció interna perquè les publicacions oficials relatives a agents de la GUB s’adapti a la protecció de dades personals especial que correspon segons la llei. També et pot interessar La Guàrdia Urbana incorpora 60 agents: “Us necessitem al carrer i al servei de la ciutadania” Javier Arilla 2 minuts de lectura “Una gravetat extraordinària” Pel que fa a la denúncia interposada davant de l’Autoritat Catalana de Protecció de Dades (APDCAT) pels sindicats SIP-FEPOL i CSIF , Batlle ha dit que el cas encara està en la fase inicial d’investigació i que l’Ajuntament oferirà tota la col·laboració necessària. També ha assegurat que, ara per ara, “no consta que s’hagi fet cap ús indegut o delictiu de la informació publicada”. Sigui com sigui, els partits de l’oposició en bloc han retret durament al govern municipal de Jaume Collboni la filtració de les dades personals dels 1.245 agents de la Guàrdia Urbana. Jordi Martí (Junts) ha qualificat els fets “d’incident d’una gravetat extraordinària ” i Gonzalo de Oro (Vox) ha avisat que tot plegat “ ha posat en perill la nostra Guàrdia Urbana”. Marc Serra (BComú) ha reclamat a l’executiu del PSC que “cal garantir que no torni a succeir ” una filtració de dades personals de la GUB i Jordi Coronas (ERC) ha exigit que “ s’elimini qualsevol rastre a internet de les dades publicades”. Sonia Devesa (PP) ha reblat que la filtració “pot comportar riscos per als agents afectats i les seves famílies “. Un parell de cotxes patrulla de la Guàrdia Urbana

Aquest ball de gegants i bèsties és el ritual inaugural de les festes de Barcelona i se celebra des de l’any 1993. El Toc d’inici es fa el dimecres 23 de setembre a la plaça de Sant Jaume a les 20 h i si no podeu anar a viure’l en primera persona, el podreu seguir en directe a betevé , en un programa especial tot coincidint amb el tret de sortida les festes. articles.body: El Barça rebrà el Racing de Santander aquest dimecres a partir de les 21.30 h en partit corresponent a la sisena jornada de Lliga i ho farà pendent del cel… i dels mòbils . La pluja intensa prevista per a l’hora del partit podria provocar que se suspengués l’enfrontament . Però què ha de passar perquè se suspengui? Protecció Civil ha d’enviar un ES-Alert Ara mateix, durant el matí de dimecres, estem en alerta 4/6 per risc de pluges , però si posteriorment el Meteocat l’acabés apujant a grau 5/6 i Protecció Civil ho considerés convenient, podria enviar un ES-Alert als telèfons mòbils de la gent que viu a les zones alertades. Aquest ES-Alert demanaria evitar desplaçaments i activitats a l’aire lliure, com, per exemple, el partit del Barça contra el Racing al Camp Nou. Ara bé, Protecció Civil assegura que el fet d’enviar un ES-Alert no implica, directament, que se suspengui el partit . Creuen que s’hauria d’estudiar perquè no ha coincidit mai un ES-Alert amb un partit de futbol que arrossegui tant de públic. Protecció Civil demana estar pendents de la roda de premsa que es farà aquest dimecres a les 12.30 h , però creuen que, segons les prediccions meteorològiques actuals, no s’enviarà aquest ES-Alert. També et pot interessar El Camp Nou acollirà la final de la Champions del 2029: l’estadi blaugrana s’imposa a Wembley Pablo Agudo 1 minut de lectura El precedent del Vila-real – Espanyol En tot cas, sí que es pot suspendre un partit de Lliga per pluges fortes . L’exemple el va patir l’ Espanyol el març del 2025, tant l’equip com els aficionats que es van desplaçar fins a Vila-real . L’enfrontament es va cancel·lar quan les portes de l’Estadi de la Ceràmica ja estaven obertes. De fet, la decisió es va prendre just abans de començar, amb els jugadors ja vestits i a punt de saltar al terreny de joc . Com funciona l’ES-Alert L’ ES-Alert és un sistema d’ avisos massius que s’envien als telèfons mòbils localitzats en una zona geogràfica concreta . Forma part de l’adopció feta per l’Estat espanyol, el febrer del 2023, de la Directiva europea  (2018/1972), que imposa als països membres de la UE tenir un  sistema d’alertes per a telefonia mòbil . El sistema està dissenyat per assegurar la difusió d’alertes perquè la ciutadania segueixi unes instruccions concretes de manera immediata  per  protegir-se i evitar danys  si es troben en una zona afectada per un  accident greu , una  catàstrofe  o qualsevol altra  situació crítica d’emergència .
